evidence.title: Evaluating and Validating Large Language Models for Health Education on Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip: 2-Phase Study With Expert Ratings and a Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial
evidence.outcome: eHealth literacy and DDH knowledge after structured LLM training vs web search
evidence.effect: eHEALS group difference 1.73 (0.49-2.97) at T1 and 2.40 (1.13-3.67) at T2. DDH knowledge d=0.71 at T1 and 0.54 at T2. The group×time interaction was nonsignificant (P=.26).
evidence.quote: The intervention group showed higher scores than the control group at T1 (33.62, 95% CI 32.76-34.49; d =0.20, 95% CI 0.13-0.56) and T2 (33.27, 95% CI 32.38-34.17; d =0.36, 95% CI 0.01-0.80), indicating sustained improvements following the LLM-generated learning intervention.

evidence.title: A community-codesigned LLM-powered chatbot for primary care: a randomized controlled trial
evidence.outcome: Gap between self-reported and objective health awareness (overconfidence)
evidence.effect: Health awareness gap reduced: 0.83 ± 1.62 in e-learning group vs 1.37 ± 1.55 in consultation-only (P < 0.001).
evidence.quote: This gap was significantly reduced in the e-learning group compared with the consultation-only group (0.83 ± 1.62 versus 1.37 ± 1.55; P < 0.001).

evidence.title: Can co-designed educational interventions help consumers think critically about asking ChatGPT health questions? Results from a randomised-controlled trial
evidence.outcome: Intention to ask ChatGPT higher-risk health questions, ChatGPT knowledge, and trust after brief AI health literacy interventions vs control
evidence.effect: Both intervention groups had lower intention for higher-risk scenarios vs control (animation M=2.42, images M=2.69, control M=3.12; p<0.001), higher ChatGPT knowledge (p<0.001), and lower trust (p<0.001). No effect on lower-risk intentions (p=0.800).
evidence.quote: Participants in both intervention groups reported lower intentions to use ChatGPT for higher risk scenarios compared to control (n=205, M=3.12/5, 95%CI: 2.98 to 3.27, p<0.001).

evidence.title: Influence of AI Chatbot Use on Healthcare-Seeking Behavior among Outpatient Clinic Visitors of Two Healthcare Institutions in Northern Cyprus: A Cross-Sectional Study
evidence.outcome: Patient trust in AI chatbot health answers and effect on care-seeking
evidence.effect: 73.7% used AI for health questions; trust low (31.9%), 47.5% unsure; AI delayed doctor visits in 22.5% and encouraged visits in 43.2%.
evidence.quote: AI delayed doctor visits in 22.5% while encouraging visits in 43.2%.

commentary.bottom_line: Three randomized trials suggest that structured AI or eHealth literacy education may raise literacy scores and knowledge and reduce overconfidence and intended risky chatbot use, though all measured short-term surrogate outcomes. Whether this education prevents harm from AI or online misinformation has not been tested.

perspectives.view: Three trials tested education, two in real deployment in China and one simulated in Australia, and all favored it. Certainty is low because outcomes were surrogates and the interventions differed. In the Chinese caregiver trial, the eHEALS difference was 1.73 at T1 and 2.40 at T2, but the group-by-time interaction was nonsignificant (P=.26).

In the Australian trial, brief animation or image interventions lowered intention to ask ChatGPT higher-risk questions (M=2.42 and 2.69 vs 3.12 for control) and left lower-risk intentions unchanged. A survey in Northern Cyprus found that AI delayed doctor visits for 22.5% of users. No trial measured delayed care or harm, so the safety benefit remains inferred.

The largest trial enrolled 2113 participants in a real deployment and found that e-learning narrowed the gap between self-rated and objective health awareness (0.83 vs 1.37, P<0.001). None of the trials reported staff time, delivery cost, or how education fit into clinical workflows, so fidelity and burden at scale are unknown.

The 2113-participant trial in China included rural, older, low health literacy, racial or ethnic minority, and non-English-speaking participants. No trial enrolled Medicaid or US safety-net patients. The results may not transfer to US populations whose language access, device access, and trust in institutions differ.

In the Northern Cyprus survey, 73.7% of 2825 patients and companions used AI for health questions and 47.5% were unsure whether to trust it. The Australian trial found that education lowered trust in ChatGPT. Lower trust may protect patients if it prompts them to contact a clinician, but no trial tested whether they did.

commentary.research_gap: No trial has tested whether AI literacy education reduces patient harm or delayed care, or whether it increases contact with clinicians. None was conducted in a US health system or measured delivery cost and staff burden. Trials with longer follow-up and behavioral or clinical outcomes would address these gaps.
commentary.underserved_note: One trial of 2113 participants in China included limited or non-English-speaking, low health literacy, rural, older, and minority participants and found reduced overconfidence. No test included Medicaid or safety-net populations. The finding suggests education may reach low-literacy groups, but its effect in US safety-net settings is untested.
